comments.author: @aaronstathatos6195
comments.text:
As someone who uses Cursor with an O3 Mini model, I can attest it’s fine for simpler tasks like building UIs or following basic coding instructions. However, it quickly runs into trouble with updated libraries because it was trained on now-deprecated code—something even RAG-based documentation can’t fully fix. As your codebase grows and interdependencies become more complex, the model often ends up breaking one thing while fixing another—or adding or removing functionality you never asked for. Sure, it might pull off something like a black hole simulation in Python, but once you’re dealing with a more complex stack that spans multiple languages, it really struggles. 

All that being said…. I have a combination of doubts and optimism

comments.author: @zxwxz
comments.text: The real comparison should be between cost and effectiveness. If O3 can surpass O1-ioi with just 50 samples, while O1-ioi requires 10K samples to select 50 samples, then we need to compare the inference costs of both. We can temporarily ignore the training or development costs here. If a general LRM can directly defeat a specialized LRM, it is very optimistic for the future of scaling laws. This is because specialized RL fields have always required special human experts and are difficult to scale, which is entirely different in complexity from training with a large number of GPUs. In fact, humans have always been the biggest bottleneck in the expansion laws. I believe that what LRM needs the most is to specialize different TTC times for different levels of problems to dynamically save operational costs. For example, simple programs should automatically call O3-mini, while more complex problems should call O3. Otherwise, the rapidly increasing operational costs of future models will also be a significant burden.
